title: Implicit Conversion on a Join Key
description: Joining a VARCHAR key to an INT column converts every row and scans; align the types so the join can seek its index. Why it matters: mismatched key types between joined tables are a common legacy-schema problem, and this is exactly why a join that should be instant scans millions of rows instead.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

This lesson is about a mismatch that's incredibly easy to introduce by accident and shockingly expensive once it happens: joining two tables on a "key" column where one side stores it as text and the other stores it as a number. In this lesson, `Orders.CustomerCode` is a `VARCHAR(10)` (text), while `Customers.CustomerId` is an `INT` (a number) — and joining them, even to look up a single customer, ends up scanning all 300,000 rows in `Orders` instead of doing a quick, targeted lookup.

To understand why, you need to know a rule SQL Server (and most databases) follows called **data type precedence**. Whenever two values of different data types need to be compared (like in a `JOIN ... ON` clause or a `WHERE` clause), the database can't compare "apples to oranges" directly — it has to convert one side to match the other's type first. SQL Server has a documented ranking of which types "outrank" others, and when types differ, the *lower-ranked* type gets silently converted to the *higher-ranked* type. Numeric types like `INT` outrank text types like `VARCHAR`. So when you compare `CustomerCode` (text) to `CustomerId` (a number), SQL Server doesn't convert the number to text — it converts the *text* to a number instead, because `INT` wins the precedence contest.

Here's where it gets expensive. This conversion has to happen *before* the comparison can be evaluated — which means, logically, SQL Server needs to convert `CustomerCode` to a number for every single row in `Orders`, not just the one row you're actually interested in. And a converted/computed value isn't something the existing index on `CustomerCode` (which is sorted by the original *text* values) can help with — the index is sorted by strings like `"C0001"`, `"C0002"`, `"C0100"`, but the query needs to compare *numeric conversions* of those strings, and the index has no pre-computed, sorted list of "what each of these text values looks like once converted to a number." So exactly like a function wrapped around a column (covered elsewhere in this course), an implicit conversion applied to the *indexed* column makes that column's index useless for seeking — SQL Server has to scan every row, convert it, and check the result, one row at a time, instead of jumping straight to the answer.

This is exactly why it's called an **implicit** conversion: nobody wrote `CAST()` or `CONVERT()` anywhere in the query — it's something SQL Server does silently, behind the scenes, to make the comparison type-valid. That's what makes this bug so sneaky: the query *looks* completely normal (`... ON o.CustomerCode = c.CustomerId ...`), it runs and returns correct results, and there is no visible sign in the SQL text itself that anything expensive is happening. You only discover it by looking at the actual execution plan and noticing a scan where you expected a seek, or by noticing a small "CONVERT_IMPLICIT" warning/operator hidden in the plan details.

The root cause here is almost always a schema design mismatch between systems — one team or one system stores customer keys as auto-incrementing integers, another team (or an older legacy system, or an import from an external partner) stores them as formatted text codes. It's an extremely common situation in real companies where systems get integrated after being built independently, and it becomes a permanent landmine sitting in the schema until someone specifically goes looking for it.

The fix comes in a couple of flavors depending on the situation: you can't change data type precedence, but you *can* control which side gets converted, and you can choose to convert the *small*, already-filtered side of the query instead of the *huge* side. In this lesson's case, since you're already filtering down to `CustomerId = 100` (a single customer), you can explicitly convert that one known value to text yourself — comparing `CustomerCode = CAST(100 AS VARCHAR(10))` — so the conversion happens once, on one known value, rather than 300,000 times across the whole `Orders` table. The truly durable fix, though, is to align the column types properly at the schema level so no conversion is ever needed at all.

Why does this matter? Because type mismatches between joined tables are one of the most common "legacy schema" problems in real production systems, they produce completely correct query results (so nobody notices from testing alone), and the performance cost is invisible unless you specifically check the execution plan. It's a great example of why "the query returns the right answer" and "the query performs well" are two entirely separate questions.

A useful mental habit here is to think of every join condition as implicitly asking "are these two values directly comparable, or does one of them need to change shape first?" Whenever two tables were built by different teams, at different times, or migrated from different source systems, it's worth explicitly checking the data types of any column you plan to join on — not just its name. Two columns can share an identical name and an identical real-world meaning ("the customer's identifier") and still be stored completely differently under the hood. This mismatch tends to survive for a surprisingly long time in real systems, because nobody notices during development (small test data makes everything fast regardless), and the query keeps returning correct results forever — the only symptom is performance, and only once the tables get large enough for the wasted, per-row conversion work to actually matter. If you're ever debugging "why is this specific join slow, when the same shape of join elsewhere in the codebase is fast," checking whether the joined columns have matching data types is one of the fastest, highest-value things to rule out early.

A final practical tip: SQL Server Management Studio and Azure Data Studio both let you hover over a join operator in a graphical execution plan and see a warning icon plus tooltip text mentioning an implicit conversion, which is often the very first clue that leads a developer to discover this exact class of bug. Getting into the habit of actually reading these warning icons, rather than skipping past them, pays off considerably over time.

## Scenario
`Orders` stores the customer key as text (`CustomerCode VARCHAR(10)`, indexed), while `Customers.CustomerId` is an `INT`. Joining them for one customer — `... JOIN Customers c ON o.CustomerCode = c.CustomerId WHERE c.CustomerId = 100` — scans all 300,000 orders even though `IX_Orders_CustomerCode` should make it a tiny seek.

## Why it's slow
The join compares `VARCHAR` to `INT`. SQL Server resolves the mismatch using **data type precedence**: `INT` outranks `VARCHAR`, so it converts the *lower*-precedence side — `o.CustomerCode` — to `INT`. The predicate effectively becomes `CONVERT(INT, o.CustomerCode) = 100`. That wraps the indexed column in a function, so `IX_Orders_CustomerCode` can no longer be **sought**: the plan degrades to an **Index Scan**, converting every code to check it. (SQL Server usually flags this with a *CardinalityEstimate / PlanAffectingConvert* warning.)

## What to look for
- An **Index Scan** (not Seek) on the large table's join column.
- A type mismatch between the two join columns (`VARCHAR` vs `INT`).

## The concept
Keep the indexed column **bare** and convert the *other* side instead. Cast `c.CustomerId` down to `VARCHAR(10)` so the comparison is `VARCHAR = VARCHAR`: the constant is converted once, and SQL Server **seeks** `IX_Orders_CustomerCode` for the matching code. Reads on `Orders` fall from ~1,000 to a handful. The durable fix is to store join keys in matching types in the first place.
startingQuery: SELECT o.OrderId, o.Total FROM Orders o JOIN Customers c ON o.CustomerCode = c.CustomerId WHERE c.CustomerId = 100;
hints: The join compares VARCHAR (CustomerCode) to INT (CustomerId); type precedence converts the VARCHAR column to INT.
Converting the indexed column wraps it in a function, so it can only be scanned, not sought.
Cast the INT side down to VARCHAR(10) so the indexed CustomerCode column stays bare and can be seeked.
